tagline: Glamorous Costa del Sol resort town of yacht marinas, sun-soaked beaches, and whitewashed old-town charm

taxi.fareNote: Official white taxis with a diagonal stripe run regulated meters set by the town hall; fixed fares apply to Málaga airport runs, so confirm the rate before departure

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU emergency number covering police, fire, and ambulance; 091 reaches the National Police directly

hood_desc: Marbella's medieval old town of narrow whitewashed lanes centered on the flower-filled Plaza de los Naranjos. Packed with tapas bars, boutiques, and the town's oldest church, it's the most walkable and historic base.
The famed marina lined with superyachts, designer boutiques, and rooftop clubs that put Marbella on the jet-set map. Nightlife and people-watching here run late and glossy.
A beachfront strip of five-star resorts, private villas, and palm-lined avenues connecting the old town to Puerto Banús. Home to some of Spain's most exclusive hotels.
An inland residential district built around golf courses, popularly nicknamed the 'Golf Valley.' Quiet, leafy, and geared toward longer-stay visitors and expats.
A relaxed seaside town just west of Marbella with a long promenade, family beaches, and a growing food scene, popular with locals seeking a lower-key alternative.

transit.pay: Cash or card onboard; multi-trip cards available at kiosks
transit.note: No rail or metro; buses run along the coast to San Pedro and Puerto Banús, but most visitors rely on taxis, rideshare, or rental cars

train: No station in Marbella; nearest is Málaga María Zambrano, ~50 km away
bus: Frequent Avanza coaches along the coast to Málaga, Fuengirola, and Estepona

tip.r: Rounding up or leaving 5-10% at restaurants is appreciated but not obligatory; service is not usually included

tagline: Bavarian wine city crowned by a UNESCO prince-bishops' Residence and the Old Main Bridge

taxi.fareNote: Traditional cream-colored taxis operate metered fares regulated by the city; ranks are at the Hauptbahnhof and Marktplatz

emergency.note: 110 reaches police, 112 reaches fire and ambulance services; both are toll-free nationwide

hood_desc: The compact historic core packed with the Würzburg Residence, Marienberg Fortress views, and the Old Main Bridge lined with wine stands. Almost everything worth seeing is within walking distance here.
A riverside district across the Main, overlooked by the Käppele pilgrimage church on its hillside vineyards. Quieter and residential, with easy footpaths up to panoramic viewpoints.
A leafy residential quarter south of downtown bordering the Ringpark, popular with families and known for tidy streets and small local shops.
Home to the University of Würzburg's main campus, giving the area a young, café-and-bar energy with a steady student population.
A working-class district around the main train station, convenient for arrivals and offering some of the city's better-value accommodation.

transit.pay: VVM zone tickets from machines, app, or onboard; day passes available
transit.note: Compact tram-and-bus network makes most sights reachable without a car; the Altstadt itself is pedestrian-friendly

train: Würzburg Hauptbahnhof is a major ICE hub on the Frankfurt-Nuremberg-Munich line, ~1h15 to Frankfurt
bus: Regional buses and the Romantic Road coach route

car.idp: Not required for EU visitors, recommended for others

tip.r: Round up or add roughly 5-10%, stating the total aloud when paying rather than leaving cash on the table

tagline: Guatemala's highland second city, a colonial center for Spanish schools and volcano treks

taxi.fareNote: Taxis lack meters, so agree on a fare before departure; tuk-tuks (mototaxis) are the cheapest way to cover short distances around town

emergency.note: 110 reaches the National Civil Police (PNC), 123 reaches Bomberos Voluntarios for fire and ambulance; response outside the center can be slow

hood_desc: The neoclassical heart of Xela, centered on the grand Parque Centro América and its columned Passage. Cafés, language schools, and the cathedral cluster within a few blocks here.
A bustling working-class zone built around its namesake market, known for cheap eats, everyday commerce, and easy access to intercity bus terminals.
A semi-rural district on the city's edge that serves as the main gateway for hikes up Santa María and Santiaguito volcanoes. Quiet and sparsely built up.
A hillside residential area prized for panoramic views over the valley, popular with longer-term language-school students renting rooms with local families.
A mixed residential and commercial zone housing the Teatro Municipal and several markets, offering a more local, less touristed slice of the city.

transit.pay: Cash only, paid to driver or fare collector
transit.map: No official transit map; routes are learned locally or via word of mouth
transit.note: No metro or formal rail; the walkable center covers most needs, with tuk-tuks and minibuses for outlying areas

air: La Aurora International Airport (GUA), main gateway
train: No passenger rail service in Guatemala
bus: Extensive Pullman and 'chicken bus' network to Guatemala City (~4 hrs) and surrounding highland towns

tip.r: Around 10% at sit-down restaurants is customary; small change for tuk-tuk or taxi drivers is welcomed but not required

tagline: Ancient souqs, olive-oil soap, and the sweetest kanafeh in the Middle East

taxi.fareNote: Shared 'service' taxis run fixed routes for a small flat fare; private taxis should agree on a price or confirm the meter before riding.

emergency.note: The Palestine Red Crescent Society runs ambulance service (101); police and medical response times can be affected by checkpoints and access restrictions.

hood_desc: The heart of Nablus, a dense Ottoman-era souq of stone alleys, soap factories, spice stalls, and kanafeh shops that has been continuously inhabited for centuries. Landmarks like the Great Mosque and several 18th-century hammams sit alongside working soap workshops.
A leafier, more modern district west of downtown, home to An-Najah National University and many of the city's newer cafes, shops, and apartment buildings favored by students and professionals.
Named for its natural springs, this older neighborhood on the western edge of the Old City has traditional stone houses and quieter streets, with views up toward Mount Gerizim.

The mountain overlooking the city from the south, home to a small Samaritan community at Kiryat Luza and ancient ruins including a ruined Byzantine church; reachable by road with sweeping views over Nablus.
The commercial center of the newer city, anchored by Al-Manara clock tower square, with banks, shops, and the busiest streets for everyday city life outside the Old City.

transit.map: no official app; ask locally or hotel staff for routes
transit.note: There is no fixed public transit map; shared 'service' taxis are the main way to get around and between towns.

air: No airport; nearest is Ben Gurion Airport (TLV) in Israel
train: No rail service in the West Bank
bus: Regular service taxis and buses connect Nablus to Ramallah, Jenin, and other West Bank cities

airport.name: Ben Gurion Airport (TLV)
rentals: Not available locally; arranged via Israeli airport agencies

tip.r: Tipping is not customary; rounding up a bill or leaving small change for good service is appreciated but not required.

tagline: A perfectly preserved medieval old town on the Danube, sausages and all

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered and reliable but pricier than public transit; ranks are found at the train station and Old Town squares.

emergency.note: 112 reaches both fire and ambulance services anywhere in Germany; 110 is the general police line.

hood_landmark.Stadtamhof: Northern end of the Stone Bridge

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed medieval core, packed with Gothic towers, the Stone Bridge, the cathedral, and the Wurstkuchl sausage kitchen; nearly car-free and best explored on foot.
A small, quiet quarter just across the Danube from the Altstadt, with its own village-like main street, church, and river views back toward the old town.
An up-and-coming riverside district east of the center with parks, indie bars, and a younger, more relaxed vibe than the historic core.
A residential district south of the center with Roman-era remains, local bakeries, and everyday German neighborhood life away from the tourist crowds.
Home to the University of Regensburg campus, with student bars, budget eats, and a livelier nightlife scene than the historic center.

transit.hours: roughly 4:30am-1am, with limited night buses on weekends
transit.pay: RVV tickets via app, machines, or onboard; day passes available
transit.note: Regensburg is famously the largest German city without a tram network; buses cover the whole city well and the Altstadt is walkable end to end.

train: Regensburg Hauptbahnhof has frequent ICE/regional connections to Munich, Nuremberg, and Frankfurt
bus: FlixBus connects Regensburg to major German cities

tip.r: Round up the bill or add roughly 5-10%, handed directly to the server rather than left on the table.

tagline: Japan's most storied hot-spring town, steaming beside the Yubatake

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are clean, safe, and expensive by distance; most visitors get around on foot or by the town's onsen loop bus instead.

emergency.note: 119 covers both ambulance and fire; some English support is available on emergency lines in this tourist area.

hood_desc: The steaming, sulfur-scented heart of town, built around the wooden troughs of the Yubatake where hot spring water cascades and glows at night; ryokan, shops, and foot baths ring the square.
A wooded park a short walk uphill from the center, with free open-air baths tucked among the trees and a peaceful, forested atmosphere away from the main crowds.
A quieter residential onsen district with small local bathhouses used more by residents than tourists, offering an everyday, unpolished side of the town.
The main shopping street lined with souvenir shops, izakaya, and the Netsu-no-Yu bathhouse, where staff perform the traditional 'yumomi' water-cooling dance.
The edge of town where the road climbs toward Mt. Kusatsu-Shirane's volcanic crater lake, popular for hiking and ropeway views in warmer months.

transit.pay: cash or IC card on board
transit.map: available at the tourist information center near the Yubatake
transit.note: The town center is compact and walkable; the loop bus mainly helps reach outlying ryokan and the ropeway.

air: No local airport; nearest is Tokyo Haneda (HND)
train: JR Naganohara-Kusatsuguchi Station, then a 25-minute connecting bus into town
bus: Direct highway buses run from Tokyo (Shinjuku/Ikebukuro), about 4 hours

tip.r: Tipping is not practiced and can cause confusion; excellent service is simply the norm, included in the price.

tagline: Europe's oldest city, wrapped by Atlantic beaches and Carnival spirit.

taxi.fareNote: Official white taxis with a red stripe; fares are metered with surcharges for night, weekends, luggage, and airport/station pickups.

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU emergency number covering police, fire, and ambulance.

hood_desc: Cadiz's oldest quarter, wedged inside three medieval Roman-era gates, with narrow lanes leading to the excavated Teatro Romano. It feels like a living archaeological site, with faded facades and quiet, atmospheric plazas.

The fiercely traditional fishing barrio that is the beating heart of Cadiz's famous Carnival, packed with tiny tapas bars and freidurias serving fried fish straight from the bay. It backs onto Playa de la Caleta, the city's most photogenic beach.

A working-class neighborhood long associated with flamenco, home to intimate peñas (flamenco clubs) where you can hear authentic cante flamenco. It's grittier and less touristy than the surrounding old town.

A lively, central district built around the Gran Teatro Falla and bustling squares like Plaza de la Merced, mixing everyday local life with theatre-going crowds. Its markets and shops make it a good base for exploring on foot.
The postcard beach neighborhood between two 16th-century castles, Santa Catalina and San Sebastian, where locals swim, stroll the seafront promenade, and watch the Atlantic sunset.

transit.pay: Cash or contactless on TUC city buses; ferry tickets bought at the dock
transit.note: The old town is compact and best explored on foot; a small passenger ferry (El Vapor) crosses the bay to El Puerto de Santa Maria.

train: High-speed AVE/Avant and regional trains to Seville and Madrid from Cadiz station
bus: ALSA intercity coaches to Seville, Malaga, and beyond
ferry: Local passenger ferry (El Vapor) to El Puerto de Santa Maria

tip.r: Rounding up or leaving 5-10% for good service is appreciated but not expected; service charge is included in prices.

tagline: The Ottoman Empire's second capital, crowned by Sinan's masterpiece mosque.

taxi.fareNote: Yellow taxis are metered ('taksimetre'); confirm the meter is running, as short tourist trips are sometimes negotiated flat-rate instead.

emergency.note: 112 is the unified national emergency number in Türkiye, covering police, ambulance, and fire.

hood_landmark.Karaagac: Lausanne Monument and old Karaagac train station
hood_landmark.Sarayici: Kirkpinar wrestling arena and Edirne Palace ruins

hood_desc: Edirne's historic core, dominated by Mimar Sinan's UNESCO-listed Selimiye Mosque and the older Uc Serefeli and Eski Camii mosques. Cobbled streets are lined with Ottoman-era shops, tea houses, and the covered bazaar.

A leafy district just across the Meric River, once the terminus of the Orient Express line; the old train station now houses a university fine arts faculty. Riverside parks and the Lausanne Monument make it a peaceful escape from the center.

An island in the Tunca River that once held the sprawling Edirne Palace, now largely ruins, and today hosts the centuries-old Kirkpinar oil-wrestling festival each summer. It's a quieter, green area popular for walks along the water.

A residential neighborhood spreading north of the center, mixing everyday apartment blocks with local markets and neighborhood mosques. It offers a glimpse of ordinary Edirne life away from the monuments.
A mixed commercial-residential district with small shops, bakeries, and produce markets serving locals rather than tourists. It sits within easy walking or a short dolmus ride of the historic center.

transit.map: Edirne Belediyesi municipal bus route maps
transit.note: Edirne's historic core is small and very walkable; dolmus minibuses cover outer neighborhoods and nearby villages.

train: Limited passenger rail; most travelers use intercity buses

tip.r: A small tip of 5-10% in restaurants is appreciated; rounding up taxi fares is common.

tagline: Japan's steaming onsen capital, where the earth itself boils over.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis have automatic rear doors and are metered; fares run higher late at night, and having your destination written in Japanese helps since drivers rarely speak English.

emergency.note: 110 for police, 119 for ambulance/fire; a multilingual tourist support hotline is also available.

hood_desc: The most famous onsen district, built directly around the sulfurous steam vents of the 'Jigoku' (hells), a cluster of surreal, colorfully mineral-stained hot springs open for viewing. Steam rises from drains and vents throughout the neighborhood, and jigoku-mushi steam-cooked food stalls are everywhere.

The commercial heart of the city around Beppu Station, with the retro public bathhouse Takegawara Onsen, shopping arcades, and easy access to trains and buses. It's the most convenient base for first-time visitors.

A hillside hot-spring hamlet famous for its thatched-roof yunohana steam huts, where mineral crystals are harvested from the steam for bath salts. The sulfur smell and misty hillside views give it a distinctly otherworldly atmosphere.

A quieter, more local onsen town north of central Beppu, known for Shibaseki Onsen, a rustic bathhouse built right into the tidal rocks on the beach. It's popular with residents rather than tour groups.

A residential onsen neighborhood in the hills above the city, home to Hyotan Onsen, a beloved public bathhouse with an outdoor gourd-shaped pool, waterfall bath, and sand bath. It offers sweeping views over Beppu Bay.

transit.hours: Kamenoi Bus runs roughly 6:00-22:00; JR trains keep similar hours
transit.note: Kamenoi Bus's Jigoku Meguri loop line links Beppu Station to the Kannawa hot-spring hell district.

train: JR Nippo Main Line; limited express 'Sonic' service to Fukuoka/Kokura and local trains to Oita
bus: Highway buses to Fukuoka, Kumamoto, and Oita
ferry: Overnight Sunflower ferry service to Osaka/Kobe

airport.name: Oita Airport (OIT)
airport.drive: 45 min by limousine bus, or about 30 min by high-speed boat

tip.r: Tipping is not part of Japanese culture and can even cause confusion; excellent service is already the standard and included in the price.
